question: A legal team wants Claude to draft a contract clause and needs the tone to closely match previously approved clauses in structure and phrasing. They have three approved clauses available. What is the best way to use these in the prompt?
options: A) Include only one of the three approved clauses and drop the other two
B) Summarize the general topic of the three clauses in one sentence instead of their text
C) Describe the desired tone abstractly without showing any approved clause
D) Include the three approved clauses as examples wrapped in tags to mirror phrasing
correct_answers: D) Include the three approved clauses as examples wrapped in tags to mirror phrasing
explanations: Incorrect. Dropping two of the three approved examples reduces the diversity of reference material, risking a narrower or less representative match to approved style.
Incorrect. A one-sentence summary discards the actual structure and phrasing details that the legal team wants the new clause to match.
Incorrect. An abstract tone description without concrete examples is a weaker way to steer close structural and phrasing alignment than showing the actual approved clauses.

Correct. Providing the relevant approved clauses as examples wrapped in example tags mirrors the actual use case and lets Claude closely match their structure and phrasing, the recommended approach for steering tone and format.
